summary: Fills a gap in the IPv6 socket APIs by adding socket options and getaddrinfo flags that let applications influence source address selection. It builds on RFC 3484 default address selection. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A way for a program to say which of its own addresses it would like to use.

questions: ipv6 socket api source address selection
how to choose source address ipv6
how to prefer temporary ipv6 source address
subtitle: Socket options that let an application nudge which of its own IPv6 addresses is used as the source.

tldr.problem: RFC 3484 sets default rules for choosing IPv6 source addresses and says applications should be able to reverse some of them, but no socket API existed for that.
tldr.mechanism: A new IPV6_ADDR_PREFERENCES socket option and matching getaddrinfo() flags let applications state preferences such as temporary vs. public, home vs. care-of, and CGA vs. non-CGA, while the system applies the rest of the default rules.
tldr.outcome: Applications can express preferences, not hard requirements. Those that need a guarantee can use the bind2addrsel() and inet6_is_srcaddr() calls to check the result. The document is Informational.

today: RFC 5014 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes an API that builds on RFC 3484 and RFC 3493.

sections.title: Why Applications Need a Say
sections.content:
RFC 3484 defines default address selection for IPv6. By default a public address is preferred over a temporary one, a Mobile IPv6 home address over a care-of address, and a larger scope over a smaller one. An application may want to reverse a rule. For example, a mobile node may prefer its care-of address as the source of a DNS query, since that normally gives a shorter local return path than going via the home agent. A web browser may want a temporary address while a mail server wants a public one, and a debugging tool like fping may prefer a non-CGA address to avoid the cost of Secure Neighbor Discovery.

Applications can already pick a source with bind() or the IPV6_PKTINFO option (RFC 3542), but then they must check on their own that the address suits the destination, which means reimplementing the default rules. This document lets the application state attributes it prefers and leaves the rest to the system.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a program wants a particular kind of return address. Today it would have to work everything out itself, so this gives it an easy way to just ask.

sections.title: Preferences, Not Requirements
sections.content:
The approach is to let the application specify preferences, not hard requirements. If no temporary address exists, a request to prefer one falls back to a public address. Hard requirements would be problematic: an application doing a short UDP exchange would not want to fail just because no care-of address exists, and the set of addresses may change between getaddrinfo() and sendto().

For each modifiable rule there are two flags, one for each side, such as home and care-of. Setting one flag clears its opposite. An application can choose a flag, choose the opposite flag, or set neither and keep the system default. Flags set per socket, rather than per application, were chosen because environment variables may not exist everywhere and standard libraries would otherwise be affected without the application knowing.

If a flag-set combines X and Y and Y is not available, the result has attribute X and the system default for Y. On a system with only public addresses, preferring temporary and home gives a public home address.
sections.eli5: You say what you would like, and if it is not on the shelf you get the usual one instead of nothing.

sections.title: The Preference Flags and Socket Option
sections.content:
Six flags are defined: IPV6_PREFER_SRC_HOME, IPV6_PREFER_SRC_COA, IPV6_PREFER_SRC_TMP, IPV6_PREFER_SRC_PUBLIC, IPV6_PREFER_SRC_CGA and IPV6_PREFER_SRC_NONCGA. Home and care-of, temporary and public, CGA and non-CGA are opposites. Combining a flag with its opposite is contradictory, and setting contradictory flags results in the error EINVAL.

The flags are carried by a new socket option, IPV6_ADDR_PREFERENCES, at the IPPROTO_IPV6 level, used with setsockopt() and getsockopt(). Its value is a 32-bit unsigned integer of flags and applies to all packets sent through that socket. The defaults, consistent with RFC 3484, are IPV6_PREFER_SRC_HOME, IPV6_PREFER_SRC_PUBLIC and IPV6_PREFER_SRC_CGA.

The flags map to RFC 3484 source selection rule 4 (prefer home address) and rule 7 (prefer public address). No flags were defined for the scope rules or the other destination rules, because the implementers saw no practical use.
sections.eli5: There is a small set of switches such as public or temporary, and a program flips the ones it likes. Flipping both of a pair would be silly, so that gives an error.

sections.title: Using getaddrinfo() with Preferences
sections.content:
Because getaddrinfo() may sort destinations using source address information, it must know the application's preferences too. The addrinfo structure gains an ai_eflags field at the end, to keep binary compatibility, and a new AI_EXTFLAGS flag in ai_flags tells the system to read it. If ai_eflags is zero or undefined, AI_EXTFLAGS is ignored. Contradictory flags make the call fail with EAI_BADEXTFLAGS.

An application MUST pass semantically equivalent flags to getaddrinfo() and setsockopt(); otherwise behavior is undefined. The document's example: a host has public source 1234::1:1 and temporary source 9876::1:2, and the destination has 1234::9:3 and 9876::9:4. By default 1234::9:3 is returned first. With IPV6_PREFER_SRC_TMP the order reverses.

If the application needs to restore the system defaults later, it should call getsockopt() first and put the saved value back afterwards.
sections.eli5: The program tells the phone book lookup about its preference too, so the list of places to call comes back in an order that fits.

sections.title: Implementation Notes and Validation
sections.content:
If a specific source is set with bind() or IPV6_PKTINFO, it takes precedence over the preference option. Unsupported preference flags should be silently ignored, so a host without Mobile IPv6 does not fail a call that mentions home or care-of addresses. An implementation supporting the API MUST implement both the getaddrinfo() flags and the socket option, and should support both stream and datagram sockets.

IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses are supported. The temporary and CGA flags do not apply to them, but the home and care-of flags may. The document does not encourage per-packet preferences, since selecting a source for every packet is expensive, but its Appendix A gives guidelines for implementations that want ancillary data support.

Some applications must fail rather than use the wrong kind of address. Preferences cannot guarantee that, so the document adds two functions. bind2addrsel() binds a socket to the source address that would be selected for a given destination, without sending a packet, which matters for TCP because connect() would send a SYN. inet6_is_srcaddr() then checks whether an address satisfies a set of preference flags. It returns 1 for true, 0 for false and -1 if the address is not a local one or the flags are invalid.

The steps are: pass the flags to getaddrinfo() and setsockopt(), select a source with bind2addrsel() (or connect() for UDP), read it with getsockname(), validate it, and abort if it fails. When several flags are passed, all must be satisfied.
sections.eli5:
If the program already picked an exact address, that choice wins over a mere wish.

If a program must have a certain kind of address, it picks one, looks at it, and only goes ahead if it is the right kind.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document has the same security implications as the basic IPv6 socket API (RFC 3493) and the address selection rules in RFC 3484. Letting an application prefer temporary addresses gives per-application and per-socket access to their privacy benefits. Settings such as not using a CGA or a temporary address may be restricted to privileged processes.
sections.eli5: Some choices, like skipping the extra-safe address, might only be allowed for trusted programs.
